title: The Mass (II.14)
hook: a fever, a newborn, a night shift: when the pew stays empty, Francis de Sales says you can still be there in heart
tomorrow: captain, student, granddaughter: does each need a different virtue?

segments.voice: Yesterday, aspirations: short prayers of the heart, a word or three, sent up all day long. The line was short arrows.

A fever. A newborn who finally fell asleep. A night shift that ends at dawn. A car that won't start. Sunday comes, and the usual spot in the pew stays empty. For people who love the Mass, that can sting. Francis de Sales wrote his chapter on the Mass for two readers at once: the one who walks in, and the one who can't. Can you be there from a bed? He says yes, and he says how.
screen: `A FEVER. A NEWBORN. A NIGHT SHIFT.` → `THE PEW STAYS EMPTY.` → `CAN YOU BE THERE FROM BED?`

segments.voice: First, where the Mass stands. Among all the prayers in his book, Francis gives it a place of its own: the sun of spiritual exercises, the heart of devotion. Second, how to be there. Go every day if you can, he says, so as to offer the sacrifice together with the priest. Third, how to pray through it. He walks the Mass of his day in stages and pairs each one with a moment in the life of Jesus: asking pardon at the start, his coming and his life through the readings, his teaching with the Gospel and the Creed, then his passion and death, and at Communion, the desire to be one with him, ending in thanks. Fourth, the reader who can't come. If you can't be there in body, he says, be there in heart. Choose a time, unite yourself in spirit with the Mass, and make your offering from wherever you are. Catholic teaching today says the same kind of thing about Sunday. The Catechism asks the faithful to take part in Sunday Mass, and it names illness and the care of infants among the serious reasons that excuse. So for the one in bed, the door isn't shut. It's a different door.
screen: `THE SUN OF SPIRITUAL EXERCISES.` · `OFFERED WITH THE PRIEST.` · `EACH PART, A MOMENT OF HIS LIFE.` · `ABSENT IN BODY, PRESENT IN HEART.` · then, large: `JOIN IT.`

segments.voice: Sit up and rest your hands open on your knees, palms up, as if bringing something to an altar. Through the sit, stay with one part of the Mass you know, the Gospel, the Our Father, or Communion, and be there in spirit. If you pray, join your own offering to it.
The Mass. For Francis, the center of the devout life's prayer: attended with care when you can, joined in spirit when you can't.
The line to keep: join it, from the pew or from wherever the day finds you. Be well.

howItsDone: Catholics take part in Mass on Sundays and holy days, and some go daily; those kept away by illness or caring for others often unite themselves with it in prayer, and some parishes bring them Communion.

chat.says: abuela's first sunday home and she's too weak for Mass. she's sad. what can i do from the pew?
options: Tell her when you're going so she can join in spirit from bed, and pray it for her.
Not much, honestly. If she isn't there in person, it doesn't reach her at all.
Tell her to come anyway and sit in back; missing it is worse than a fever.

notes: Introduction II.14 paraphrased: the Mass as the sun of spiritual exercises, the center of religion and heart of devotion; attend daily if possible to offer the sacrifice with the priest; the method in stages (preparation and asking pardon; Christ's coming and life up to the Gospel; his preaching and the resolve to live in the faith with the Gospel and Creed; his passion and death; desire for union at Communion; thanksgiving); if you can't be present, choose an hour (he says of the morning) to be present in spirit. Confirm the exact titles and stage divisions, which follow the Mass of his day.

CCC 2181 paraphrased: the faithful are obliged to participate in Mass on Sundays and holy days unless excused for a serious reason (for example, illness, the care of infants). Confirm the framing 'the same kind of thing' (Francis speaks of daily Mass and spiritual presence; the Catechism of the Sunday obligation and excuses); a Keeper may prefer to separate them more clearly.
The hook's examples (fever, newborn, night shift, car) are ordinary situations, not from the text.
